Chilion
KIL-ee-on
proper noun
Hebrew Kilyon, perhaps “pining” or “wasting away,” the younger son of Elimelech and the husband of Orpah.

📖 Biblical Definition

Chilion was the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi, who went with his family from Bethlehem into the country of Moab when the famine drove them out (Ruth 1:2). There he married Orpah, one of the women of Moab, and there he died, together with his brother Mahlon, leaving their mother Naomi alone in a strange land, stripped of husband and sons (Ruth 1:4–5). His wife Orpah, unlike Ruth, turned back at the parting to her own people and her gods (Ruth 1:14–15). When Boaz redeemed the family inheritance, he bought all that had been Chilion’s as well as Mahlon’s and Elimelech’s, of the hand of Naomi (Ruth 4:9). His name, which seems to mean “pining” or “wasting away,” stands beside his brother’s “sickly,” as if the very names of the two sons foretold their early graves. Chilion is remembered chiefly in contrast: his widow Orpah went back, while Mahlon’s widow Ruth clave to Naomi and to the God of Israel, and entered the lineage of the Messiah. His brief story marks the parting of two ways, where one Moabitess returned to her idols and the other pressed on to the living God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The younger son of Elimelech and Naomi, husband of Orpah, who died in Moab.

expand to see more

CHILION, the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi.

He went with his family to Moab in the famine (Ruth 1:2).

He married Orpah, a woman of Moab (Ruth 1:4).

He died in Moab with his brother Mahlon (Ruth 1:5).

Boaz redeemed all that had been Chilion’s (Ruth 4:9).

📖 Key Scripture

Ruth 1:2 — "And the name of the man was Elimelech, and the name of his wife Naomi, and the name of his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites of Bethlehemjudah. And they came into the country of Moab, and continued there."

Ruth 1:5 — "And Mahlon and Chilion died also both of them; and the woman was left of her two sons and her husband."

Ruth 4:9 — "And Boaz said unto the elders, and unto all the people, Ye are witnesses this day, that I have bought all that was Elimelech's, and all that was Chilion's and Mahlon's, of the hand of Naomi."

Ruth 1:14 — "And they lifted up their voice, and wept again: and Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his story marks the parting of two ways at the borders of Moab.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover lies in the contrast between the two widows of Elimelech’s sons. Chilion’s widow Orpah, having wept and kissed Naomi, turned back to her people and her gods; Mahlon’s widow Ruth clave to Naomi and to the LORD. The same parting hour found one returning to the idols and the other pressing on to the living God. Many come near to the kingdom and turn back; the question is whether one cleaves to the LORD or returns to the world.

Chilion’s name, “pining” or “wasting,” set beside his brother’s “sickly,” reminds the reader of the frailty of man and the certainty of death, even in the prime of life and far from home. Yet the LORD redeemed the inheritance of the dead, showing that His covenant mercy outlasts the graves of men and reaches to the generations after them.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name perhaps means “pining” or “wasting away,” paired with his brother’s name of frailty.
